title: CTS Parables of the Bible — Unit 9: Lost and Found

blocks.en: 🐑 Parables of the Bible — Unit 9: Lost and Found
blocks.es_reference: 🐑 Las Parábolas de la Biblia — Unidad 9: Perdido y Hallado

blocks.en: Professor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers
blocks.es_reference: Profesor: Dr. Wayne Cook | Director: Dr. Ted Rogers

blocks.en: "For this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found." — Luke 15:24 (NKJV)
blocks.es_reference: "Porque este mi hijo muerto era, y ha revivido; se había perdido, y es hallado." — Lucas 15:24 (RVG)

blocks.en: Orientation
blocks.es_reference: Orientación

blocks.en: For about four hundred years the Ark of the Covenant, the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the Ten Commandments, rested in the Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple. Then, when the Babylonians destroyed Jerusalem in 586 BC, it disappeared. The Bible does not tell us what happened to it. Most likely the conquerors melted it down for its gold. It has inspired treasure hunters, archaeologists, and at least one famous Hollywood film, but it has never been found.
blocks.es_reference: Durante unos cuatrocientos años el Arca del Pacto, el cofre cubierto de oro que guardaba las tablas de los Diez Mandamientos, reposó en el Lugar Santísimo del templo de Salomón. Luego, cuando los babilonios destruyeron Jerusalén en el 586 a. C., desapareció. La Biblia no nos dice qué pasó con ella. Lo más probable es que los conquistadores la fundieran por su oro. Ha inspirado a buscadores de tesoros, arqueólogos y al menos una famosa película de Hollywood, pero nunca ha sido encontrada.

blocks.en: Jesus told three stories about lost things in Luke 15, and all three have the same point: something valuable is lost, someone searches for it, and there is great joy when it is found. In Unit 1 we saw why the setting matters so much here. "Then all the tax collectors and the sinners drew near to Him to hear Him. And the Pharisees and scribes complained, saying, 'This Man receives sinners and eats with them'" (Luke 15:1–2). These three parables are Jesus' answer to that complaint. They defend His mission, and they invite the grumblers to join the celebration.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús contó tres historias sobre cosas perdidas en Lucas 15, y las tres tienen el mismo punto: algo valioso se pierde, alguien lo busca, y hay gran gozo cuando se encuentra. En la Unidad 1 vimos por qué el contexto importa tanto aquí: "Se acercaban a Jesús todos los publicanos y pecadores para oírle, y los fariseos y los escribas murmuraban, diciendo: Este a los pecadores recibe, y con ellos come" (Lucas 15:1–2). Estas tres parábolas son la respuesta de Jesús a esa queja. Defienden Su misión, e invitan a los murmuradores a unirse a la celebración.

blocks.en: I. The Lost Sheep (Luke 15:3–7)
blocks.es_reference: I. La oveja perdida (Lucas 15:3–7)

blocks.en: "What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the wilderness, and go after the one which is lost until he finds it?" (15:4). Sheep have a tendency to wander, which is why they need a shepherd. A shepherd was responsible for every animal; if one was lost, he was expected to find it or bring proof that a predator had taken it. By leaving the ninety-nine, the shepherd was not saying they were unimportant. Every sheep was dear to him. When he found the lost one, he put it on his shoulders, called his friends together, and said, "Rejoice with me." Jesus concludes, "There will be more joy in heaven over one sinner who repents than over ninety-nine just persons who need no repentance" (15:7).
blocks.es_reference: "¿Qué hombre de vosotros, teniendo cien ovejas, si pierde una de ellas, no deja las noventa y nueve en el desierto, y va tras la que se perdió, hasta encontrarla?" (15:4). Las ovejas tienden a extraviarse, y por eso necesitan un pastor. El pastor era responsable de cada animal; si uno se perdía, se esperaba que lo encontrara o que trajera prueba de que un depredador se lo había llevado. Al dejar las noventa y nueve, el pastor no decía que no importaran. Cada oveja le era querida. Cuando encontró la perdida, la puso sobre sus hombros, reunió a sus amigos y dijo: "Gozaos conmigo". Jesús concluye: "habrá más gozo en el cielo por un pecador que se arrepiente, que por noventa y nueve justos que no necesitan de arrepentimiento" (15:7).

blocks.en: The sheep was lost through its own foolishness. It simply wandered off, one mouthful of grass at a time, and nobody ever plans to be lost. Three celebrated explorers were once invited to a dinner in London. Among them they had explored Greenland, Antarctica, the Sahara, and the Amazon. They set out on foot from the Royal Geographical Society to a restaurant a quarter mile away, and within fifteen minutes they were lost in the back streets of London. Sometimes a person is lost and does not even know it.
blocks.es_reference: La oveja se perdió por su propia necedad. Simplemente se alejó, un bocado de pasto a la vez, y nadie planea perderse. Tres exploradores famosos fueron invitados una vez a una cena en Londres. Entre ellos habían explorado Groenlandia, la Antártida, el Sahara y el Amazonas. Salieron a pie de la Real Sociedad Geográfica hacia un restaurante a unos cuatrocientos metros, y en quince minutos estaban perdidos en las callejuelas de Londres. A veces una persona está perdida y ni siquiera lo sabe.

blocks.en: Jesus is concerned for those of us in the church, but He is intent on reaching those outside it. "The Son of Man has come to seek and to save that which was lost" (Luke 19:10). Evangelism professor Roy Fish told of an Indiana town of about four thousand people, where fewer than seven hundred belonged to any church. A small Baptist church held three weeks of revival meetings without stirring the slightest interest among the lost. Finally a young stonemason from Chicago, with rough manners and a foreign accent, agreed to come. He took a deacon with him and began calling at every house in town, praying with families and inviting them. Within days others joined him. Soon the building was full, the Methodists and Presbyterians were holding meetings of their own, and before it ended every lost person in town had heard the gospel two or three times. Hundreds came to Christ. The shepherd does not wait for the sheep to find its own way home; he goes after it.
blocks.es_reference: Jesús se interesa por los que estamos en la iglesia, pero está decidido a alcanzar a los que están fuera de ella. "El Hijo del Hombre vino a buscar y a salvar lo que se había perdido" (Lucas 19:10). El profesor de evangelismo Roy Fish contó de un pueblo de Indiana de unos cuatro mil habitantes, donde menos de setecientos pertenecían a alguna iglesia. Una pequeña iglesia bautista tuvo tres semanas de campaña sin despertar el menor interés entre los perdidos. Por fin un joven cantero de Chicago, de modales toscos y acento extranjero, aceptó venir. Llevó consigo a un diácono y comenzó a visitar cada casa del pueblo, orando con las familias e invitándolas. En pocos días otros se unieron a él. Pronto el templo se llenó, los metodistas y los presbiterianos tenían sus propias reuniones, y antes de terminar, cada persona perdida del pueblo había oído el evangelio dos o tres veces. Cientos vinieron a Cristo. El pastor no espera a que la oveja encuentre sola el camino a casa; va tras ella.

blocks.en: The parable also speaks to believers who have wandered. Christians of different traditions disagree about whether a true believer can lose salvation, but all agree that a believer can lose the joy of it through sin and indifference. That is why David prayed, "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation" (Psalm 51:12). Indifference may be the most miserable state a Christian can live in.
blocks.es_reference: La parábola también habla a los creyentes que se han desviado. Cristianos de distintas tradiciones no están de acuerdo sobre si un verdadero creyente puede perder la salvación, pero todos coinciden en que un creyente puede perder el gozo de ella por el pecado y la indiferencia. Por eso David oró: "Vuélveme el gozo de tu salvación" (Salmo 51:12). La indiferencia quizás sea el estado más miserable en que puede vivir un cristiano.

blocks.en: II. The Lost Coin (Luke 15:8–10)
blocks.es_reference: II. La moneda perdida (Lucas 15:8–10)

blocks.en: "Or what woman, having ten silver coins, if she loses one coin, does not light a lamp, sweep the house, and search carefully until she finds it?" (15:8). Each coin was a drachma, about a day's wage. Some interpreters suggest the coins may have been part of her dowry, perhaps even worn on a headdress as a sign that she was married, which would make the loss something like losing a wedding ring. My wife has lost her wedding rings enough times for me to understand how anxious this woman must have been. Village houses had few windows, so she lit a lamp and swept every corner until she found it. Then she too called her friends: "Rejoice with me." "Likewise, I say to you, there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner who repents" (15:10).
blocks.es_reference: "¿O qué mujer que tiene diez dracmas, si pierde una dracma, no enciende la lámpara, y barre la casa, y busca con diligencia hasta encontrarla?" (15:8). Cada dracma equivalía más o menos al salario de un día. Algunos intérpretes sugieren que las monedas quizás eran parte de su dote, tal vez llevadas en un tocado como señal de que estaba casada, lo cual haría la pérdida parecida a perder un anillo de bodas. Mi esposa ha perdido sus anillos de bodas suficientes veces como para que yo entienda cuán angustiada debió estar esta mujer. Las casas de la aldea tenían pocas ventanas, así que encendió una lámpara y barrió cada rincón hasta encontrarla. Luego también ella llamó a sus amigas: "Gozaos conmigo". "Así os digo que hay gozo delante de los ángeles de Dios por un pecador que se arrepiente" (15:10).

blocks.en: The sheep was lost through its own foolishness; the coin was lost through someone else's carelessness. The coin did not know it was lost and could not do anything to be found. Some people are lost because of the neglect of those who should have been caring for them. A newspaper once told of a diamond cutter working on a very expensive stone. He tightened the vise one more turn, and the diamond shot out, struck the ceiling, and disappeared. He locked the door and searched every corner. The owner searched with him. They never found it, and by the rules of the factory, sixty dollars a month was taken from the cutter's salary to pay for it. Six months later a repairman opened the little telephone box on the wall, and cried out, "Look what I found!" There was the diamond. Precious things we think we could never lose can be lost, and precious people can be lost right under our roof. Some Christians have lost something too: their sense of purpose. Why are you here, and what has God given you to do?
blocks.es_reference: La oveja se perdió por su propia necedad; la moneda se perdió por el descuido de otra persona. La moneda no sabía que estaba perdida y no podía hacer nada para ser hallada. Algunas personas están perdidas por el descuido de quienes debían cuidarlas. Un periódico contó una vez de un tallador de diamantes que trabajaba en una piedra muy costosa. Apretó la prensa una vuelta más, y el diamante salió disparado, pegó en el techo y desapareció. Cerró la puerta con llave y buscó en cada rincón. El dueño buscó con él. Nunca lo encontraron, y según las reglas de la fábrica, se le descontaron sesenta dólares al mes del salario para pagarlo. Seis meses después, un técnico abrió la cajita del teléfono en la pared y exclamó: "¡Miren lo que encontré!" Allí estaba el diamante. Cosas preciosas que creemos imposibles de perder pueden perderse, y personas preciosas pueden estar perdidas bajo nuestro propio techo. Algunos cristianos también han perdido algo: su sentido de propósito. ¿Por qué está usted aquí, y qué le ha dado Dios que hacer?

blocks.en: III. The Lost Son (Luke 15:11–24)
blocks.es_reference: III. El hijo perdido (Lucas 15:11–24)

blocks.en: The third story is the most famous. We call it the parable of the prodigal son. The word prodigal means wasteful. The younger son said to his father, "Father, give me the portion of goods that falls to me" (15:12). In that culture, asking for your inheritance while your father was alive was like saying, "I wish you were dead." Yet the father divided his property. The son went to a far country and wasted it all in reckless living.
blocks.es_reference: La tercera historia es la más famosa. La llamamos la parábola del hijo pródigo. La palabra pródigo significa derrochador. El hijo menor dijo a su padre: "Padre, dame la parte de los bienes que me corresponde" (15:12). En aquella cultura, pedir la herencia mientras el padre vivía era como decir: "Quisiera que estuvieras muerto." Aun así, el padre repartió sus bienes. El hijo se fue a una provincia apartada y lo desperdició todo viviendo perdidamente.

blocks.en: Then a famine came. The young Jew who had wanted freedom ended up feeding pigs, unclean animals in Jewish law, and longing to eat the pods the pigs were eating. "But when he came to himself, he said, 'How many of my father's hired servants have bread enough and to spare, and I perish with hunger!'" (15:17). He rehearsed a speech: he would confess his sin and ask to be made a hired servant.
blocks.es_reference: Entonces vino una hambruna. El joven judío que había querido libertad terminó apacentando cerdos, animales inmundos según la ley judía, y deseando comer las algarrobas que comían los cerdos. "Y volviendo en sí, dijo: ¡Cuántos jornaleros en casa de mi padre tienen abundancia de pan, y yo aquí perezco de hambre!" (15:17). Ensayó un discurso: confesaría su pecado y pediría ser tratado como un jornalero.

blocks.en: This story differs from the first two. The shepherd searched for the sheep and the woman searched for the coin, but the father did not go to the far country. It was the memory of his father's goodness that brought the boy home. "But when he was still a great way off, his father saw him and had compassion, and ran and fell on his neck and kissed him" (15:20). As we saw in Unit 1, a dignified older man in that culture did not run. This father did. The son began his speech, but the father cut him off before he could ask to be a servant. "Bring out the best robe and put it on him, and put a ring on his hand and sandals on his feet" (15:22). The robe restored his honor, the ring his authority, and the sandals his place as a son, since servants went barefoot. Then came the fatted calf and the feast: "For this my son was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found" (15:24).
blocks.es_reference: Esta historia es diferente de las dos primeras. El pastor buscó a la oveja y la mujer buscó la moneda, pero el padre no fue a la provincia apartada. Fue el recuerdo de la bondad de su padre lo que trajo al muchacho a casa. "Y cuando aún estaba lejos, lo vio su padre, y fue movido a misericordia, y corrió, y se echó sobre su cuello, y le besó" (15:20). Como vimos en la Unidad 1, en aquella cultura un hombre mayor y respetable no corría. Este padre corrió. El hijo comenzó su discurso, pero el padre lo interrumpió antes de que pudiera pedir ser jornalero: "Sacad el mejor vestido, y vestidle; y poned un anillo en su mano, y calzado en sus pies" (15:22). El vestido restauró su honra, el anillo su autoridad y el calzado su lugar como hijo, pues los siervos andaban descalzos. Luego vinieron el becerro gordo y la fiesta: "porque este mi hijo muerto era, y ha revivido; se había perdido, y es hallado" (15:24).

blocks.en: Look at the father. He was patient: the son had been gone long enough for a famine to ravage the land, yet the father saw him "a great way off," because he had never stopped watching the road. He was loving: he ran, embraced, and kissed his son before asking a single question. He was forgiving: he did not let his son finish his plea but restored him to full honor. And he had his priorities right: the most important thing was not what the son had done, but that he was alive and home.
blocks.es_reference: Mire al padre. Era paciente: el hijo había estado fuera lo suficiente para que el hambre asolara la tierra, y aun así el padre lo vio "cuando aún estaba lejos", porque nunca dejó de mirar el camino. Era amoroso: corrió, lo abrazó y lo besó antes de hacerle una sola pregunta. Era perdonador: no dejó que su hijo terminara su súplica, sino que lo restauró a plena honra. Y tenía sus prioridades en orden: lo más importante no era lo que el hijo había hecho, sino que estaba vivo y en casa.

blocks.en: A veteran missionary in China once led a talented young artist to Christ. The artist said, "I best take truth into my heart by painting it. Tell me how to paint the Christian faith." The missionary opened to Luke 15 and said, "Paint this." The artist's first painting showed the son trudging home in rags, and the father standing at the gate with his arms folded and a stern, "I told you so" look on his face. "It is beautiful," the missionary said gently, "but it misses the point. The father should be running." The artist tried again. This time the father was running down the road, robes flapping, face full of joy, and his shoes did not match: one was red and one was blue. "Why the shoes?" asked the missionary. "Because he was in such a hurry to reach his son," the artist said, "that he grabbed the nearest two shoes and ran." That is what God is like: always anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile.
blocks.es_reference: Un misionero veterano en China guió una vez a Cristo a un joven artista talentoso. El artista dijo: "Yo guardo mejor la verdad en el corazón cuando la pinto. Dígame cómo pintar la fe cristiana." El misionero abrió en Lucas 15 y le dijo: "Pinte esto." La primera pintura mostraba al hijo arrastrándose de regreso en harapos, y al padre de pie en la puerta con los brazos cruzados y una mirada severa de "te lo dije". "Es hermosa", dijo el misionero con ternura, "pero no capta el punto. El padre debería estar corriendo." El artista lo intentó de nuevo. Esta vez el padre corría por el camino, con la túnica al viento y el rostro lleno de gozo, y sus zapatos no combinaban: uno era rojo y otro azul. "¿Por qué los zapatos?", preguntó el misionero. "Porque tenía tanta prisa por llegar a su hijo", dijo el artista, "que tomó los dos primeros zapatos que encontró y corrió." Así es Dios: siempre ansioso de amar, rápido para perdonar, deseoso de reconciliar.

blocks.en: IV. The Elder Brother (Luke 15:25–32)
blocks.es_reference: IV. El hermano mayor (Lucas 15:25–32)

blocks.en: The parable does not end with the feast. The older son came in from the field, heard music and dancing, and learned why. "But he was angry and would not go in" (15:28). So the father went out to him too. The older son exploded: "Lo, these many years I have been serving you; I never transgressed your commandment at any time; and yet you never gave me a young goat, that I might make merry with my friends. But as soon as this son of yours came, who has devoured your livelihood with harlots, you killed the fatted calf for him" (15:29–30).
blocks.es_reference: La parábola no termina con la fiesta. El hijo mayor vino del campo, oyó la música y las danzas, y supo por qué. "Entonces se enojó, y no quería entrar" (15:28). Así que el padre salió también a buscarlo a él. El hijo mayor estalló: "He aquí, tantos años te sirvo, no habiéndote desobedecido jamás, y nunca me has dado ni un cabrito para gozarme con mis amigos. Pero cuando vino este tu hijo, que ha consumido tus bienes con rameras, has hecho matar para él el becerro gordo" (15:29–30).

blocks.en: Notice his words. He calls his brother "this son of yours," not "my brother." He describes his years at home as slavery: "I have been serving you." And the father gently corrects him: "Son, you are always with me, and all that I have is yours. It was right that we should make merry and be glad, for your brother was dead and is alive again, and was lost and is found" (15:31–32).
blocks.es_reference: Note sus palabras. Llama a su hermano "este tu hijo", no "mi hermano". Describe sus años en casa como esclavitud: "tantos años te sirvo". Y el padre lo corrige con ternura: "Hijo, tú siempre estás conmigo, y todas mis cosas son tuyas. Mas era necesario hacer fiesta y regocijarnos, porque este tu hermano era muerto, y ha revivido; se había perdido, y es hallado" (15:31–32).

blocks.en: This is the point of the whole chapter. The Pharisees who grumbled about Jesus eating with sinners were the elder brother. They had stayed home and kept the rules, but they did not share the Father's heart. The younger son was lost in the far country; the older son was lost at home. And the story ends without telling us whether the older brother went in to the feast. Jesus leaves that ending open because the Pharisees, and every religious person since, must write it with their own lives. There is no compassion in the elder brother, no celebration, no mismatched shoes. Bitterly he turns away, and he misses the party.
blocks.es_reference: Este es el punto de todo el capítulo. Los fariseos que murmuraban porque Jesús comía con pecadores eran el hermano mayor. Se habían quedado en casa y guardado las reglas, pero no compartían el corazón del Padre. El hijo menor se perdió en la provincia apartada; el hijo mayor se perdió en casa. Y la historia termina sin decirnos si el hermano mayor entró a la fiesta. Jesús deja abierto ese final porque los fariseos, y toda persona religiosa desde entonces, deben escribirlo con su propia vida. En el hermano mayor no hay compasión, ni celebración, ni zapatos que no combinan. Con amargura se aleja, y se pierde la fiesta.

blocks.en: V. Living in the Spirit of the Mismatched Shoes
blocks.es_reference: V. Vivir en el espíritu de los zapatos que no combinan

blocks.en: This parable shows us not only what God is like but what He wants us to be like: anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile. We can live in that spirit in three places.
blocks.es_reference: Esta parábola nos muestra no solo cómo es Dios, sino cómo quiere que seamos nosotros: ansiosos de amar, rápidos para perdonar, deseosos de reconciliar. Podemos vivir en ese espíritu en tres lugares.

blocks.en: In the church. Preaching professor Fred Craddock told about his father, who never went to church. Whenever a pastor visited, he would say, "You don't care about me. All you want is another name for your rolls and another pledge for your budget." Years later, Craddock rushed to the veterans' hospital where his father was dying of throat cancer. He could no longer speak. Craddock looked around the room and saw flowers, plants, cards, and gifts everywhere, every one of them from people at the church. His father took a pencil and wrote on a tissue box a line from Shakespeare's Hamlet: "In this harsh world draw thy breath in pain, to tell my story." "What is your story, Dad?" Craddock asked. His father wrote: "I was wrong." The church had kept right on loving him. Its shoes did not match.
blocks.es_reference: En la iglesia. El profesor de predicación Fred Craddock contó de su padre, que nunca iba a la iglesia. Cada vez que un pastor lo visitaba, decía: "A ustedes no les importo. Lo único que quieren es otro nombre para sus listas y otra promesa para su presupuesto." Años después, Craddock corrió al hospital de veteranos donde su padre moría de cáncer de garganta. Ya no podía hablar. Craddock miró alrededor del cuarto y vio flores, plantas, tarjetas y regalos por todas partes, y cada uno de ellos era de gente de la iglesia. Su padre tomó un lápiz y escribió en una caja de pañuelos una línea del Hamlet de Shakespeare: "En este mundo duro, respira con dolor para contar mi historia." "¿Cuál es tu historia, papá?", preguntó Craddock. Su padre escribió: "Me equivoqué." La iglesia había seguido amándolo. Sus zapatos no combinaban.

blocks.en: In our families. I once held a funeral for a young father named Jerry who died suddenly, leaving his wife and an eight-year-old daughter. The week before, he had given his daughter his boyhood coin collection for her birthday. It was worth perhaps sixty dollars. Three days after the funeral, Jerry's mother demanded the collection back and ordered them out of her house. When she asked me what I would do, I told her gently that she could lose her granddaughter over this, and that I would go to them at once and ask forgiveness. She looked at me with hard eyes and said, "All hell will freeze over before I would do that!" Twenty years later, her granddaughter has grown up, graduated with honors, married, and is expecting her first child, and her grandmother has not seen or spoken to her since. All because of a coin collection worth sixty dollars. That is the elder brother's spirit, and it always ends outside the feast.
blocks.es_reference: En nuestras familias. Una vez oficié el funeral de un joven padre llamado Jerry, que murió de repente, dejando a su esposa y a una hija de ocho años. La semana anterior le había regalado a su hija, por su cumpleaños, la colección de monedas que tenía desde niño. Valía quizás sesenta dólares. Tres días después del funeral, la madre de Jerry exigió que le devolvieran la colección y las echó de su casa. Cuando me preguntó qué haría yo, le dije con suavidad que podía perder a su nieta por esto, y que yo iría de inmediato a pedirles perdón. Me miró con ojos duros y dijo: "¡Primero se congelará el infierno antes de que yo haga eso!" Veinte años después, su nieta ha crecido, se graduó con honores, se casó y espera su primer hijo, y su abuela no la ha visto ni le ha hablado desde entonces. Todo por una colección de monedas que valía sesenta dólares. Ese es el espíritu del hermano mayor, y siempre termina fuera de la fiesta.

blocks.en: In our personal relationships. A minister friend told me what happened in a small town in west Arkansas. A young man named Bertram was pumping gas one Saturday morning when Old Man Jones, drunk and belligerent, began cursing him and hitting him in the back. Finally Bertram threw his arm back to push him away. The older man stumbled, tripped over a curb, struck his head on a concrete bench, and died. The whole town split into two camps. That afternoon Bertram asked the Methodist pastor to go with him to see Mrs. Jones. Relatives filled the house and yard, and no one would speak to them. When Mrs. Jones heard Bertram was there, she jumped up from her rocking chair, ran into the living room, and took both his hands. "Bertram," she said, "you don't have to say a word. I was with your mother when you were born. The doctor put you in my arms first. I know you are a good person. I know it was an accident." Then she hugged him tightly, and with that hug she healed the whole town. If we could have looked down at her feet, I think we would have seen a red house shoe and a blue house shoe. She had learned that spirit from Jesus.
blocks.es_reference: En nuestras relaciones personales. Un amigo pastor me contó lo que sucedió en un pueblito del oeste de Arkansas. Un joven llamado Bertram estaba cargando gasolina un sábado por la mañana cuando el viejo señor Jones, borracho y agresivo, comenzó a maldecirlo y a golpearlo en la espalda. Por fin Bertram echó el brazo hacia atrás para apartarlo. El anciano se tambaleó, tropezó con la banqueta, se golpeó la cabeza contra una banca de concreto y murió. Todo el pueblo se dividió en dos bandos. Esa tarde Bertram le pidió al pastor metodista que lo acompañara a ver a la señora Jones. Los parientes llenaban la casa y el patio, y nadie les dirigía la palabra. Cuando la señora Jones supo que Bertram estaba allí, se levantó de su mecedora, corrió a la sala y le tomó ambas manos. "Bertram", le dijo, "no tienes que decir nada. Yo estaba con tu madre cuando naciste. El doctor te puso primero en mis brazos. Sé que eres una buena persona. Sé que fue un accidente." Luego lo abrazó fuertemente, y con ese abrazo sanó a todo el pueblo. Si hubiéramos podido mirar sus pies, creo que habríamos visto una pantufla roja y una pantufla azul. Ella había aprendido ese espíritu de Jesús.

blocks.en: VI. Preaching Luke 15
blocks.es_reference: VI. Cómo predicar Lucas 15

blocks.en: A pastor can preach the three parables together under the theme of lost things: the sheep lost through foolishness, the coin lost through carelessness, and the son lost through willfulness, with the elder brother lost at home. Three truths run through the chapter: nobody ever plans to be lost; sometimes a person is lost and does not know it; and there is always rejoicing when the lost is found. Or the prodigal son can be preached on its own, focusing on the father who is anxious to love, quick to forgive, and eager to reconcile, and closing with the open question to the elder brothers in the congregation: will you go in?
blocks.es_reference: El pastor puede predicar las tres parábolas juntas bajo el tema de las cosas perdidas: la oveja perdida por necedad, la moneda perdida por descuido y el hijo perdido por voluntad propia, con el hermano mayor perdido en casa. Tres verdades recorren el capítulo: nadie planea perderse; a veces una persona está perdida y no lo sabe; y siempre hay gozo cuando lo perdido es hallado. O se puede predicar el hijo pródigo por sí solo, enfocándose en el padre que es ansioso de amar, rápido para perdonar y deseoso de reconciliar, y concluyendo con la pregunta abierta a los hermanos mayores de la congregación: ¿entrarás?

blocks.en: A young couple lost on a rural road once stopped to ask an old farmer where the road would take them. "Son," he said, "this road will take you anywhere in the world you want to go, if you move in the right direction." The road home to the Father is always open.
blocks.es_reference: Una joven pareja perdida en un camino rural se detuvo una vez para preguntar a un viejo agricultor adónde los llevaría el camino. "Hijo", dijo él, "este camino te llevará a cualquier parte del mundo que quieras ir, si avanzas en la dirección correcta." El camino de regreso al Padre siempre está abierto.

blocks.en: Closing
blocks.es_reference: Conclusión

blocks.en: A new mother stayed with her parents for a few days after her first baby was born. She remarked that it was surprising the baby had dark hair, since she and her husband were both fair. "Well, your daddy has black hair," her mother said. "But that doesn't matter," the daughter replied, "because I'm adopted." Her mother smiled and said the most wonderful words the daughter had ever heard: "I always forget." That is how the Father receives every prodigal who comes home. He does not hold the far country over us. He runs, He embraces, and He throws a party. "He was lost and is found."
blocks.es_reference: Una nueva madre se quedó con sus padres unos días después de nacer su primer bebé. Comentó que le sorprendía que el bebé tuviera el cabello oscuro, pues ella y su esposo eran rubios. "Bueno, tu papá tiene el cabello negro", dijo su madre. "Pero eso no importa", respondió la hija, "porque yo soy adoptada." Su madre sonrió y dijo las palabras más maravillosas que la hija había oído jamás: "Siempre se me olvida." Así recibe el Padre a cada pródigo que vuelve a casa. No nos echa en cara la provincia apartada. Corre, nos abraza y hace fiesta. "Se había perdido, y es hallado."

blocks.en:
— Dr. Wayne Cook
Chapala Theological Seminary

mc.stem: What prompted Jesus to tell the three parables of Luke 15?
options: Pharisees complaining that He received sinners and ate with them
mc.why: The parables defend Jesus' mission and invite the grumblers to the celebration (Luke 15:1–2).

mc.stem: According to this unit, all three parables in Luke 15 share which point?
options: The lost can never be found
Something valuable is lost, someone searches, and there is joy when it is found
mc.why: Joy in heaven is the common ending of all three stories.

mc.stem: The sheep was lost through:
mc.why: It wandered off one mouthful at a time; nobody ever plans to be lost.

mc.stem: The three explorers lost in London illustrate that:
options: Sometimes a person is lost and does not even know it
mc.why: Even experts can lose their way within a quarter mile of home.

mc.stem: In Roy Fish's account of the Indiana town, what finally reached the lost?
options: A stonemason going house to house with a deacon
mc.why: The shepherd does not wait for the sheep to come home; he goes after it.

mc.stem: On the question of losing salvation, this unit says:
options: Christians disagree about losing salvation, but all agree a believer can lose its joy
All Christians agree salvation can be lost
mc.why: David prayed, "Restore to me the joy of Your salvation" (Psalm 51:12).

mc.stem: The coin was lost through:
mc.why: Some people are lost because of the neglect of those who should have cared for them.

mc.stem: Some interpreters suggest the woman's ten silver coins may have been:
options: Her husband's wages for a year
Part of her dowry, perhaps worn on a headdress
mc.why: Losing one would be something like losing a wedding ring.

mc.stem: The story of the lost diamond found in the telephone box teaches that:
options: Precious things and people can be lost right under our roof
mc.why: Christians can also lose their sense of purpose.

mc.stem: In that culture, the younger son's request for his inheritance was like saying:
mc.why: Yet the father divided his property anyway.

mc.stem: How does the parable of the lost son differ from the first two?
options: The father did not go to the far country; the memory of his goodness drew the son home
The father never forgave the son
The son was lost through someone's carelessness
mc.why: The shepherd and the woman searched, but the father watched and waited.

mc.stem: The robe, ring, and sandals given to the returning son represent:
mc.why: Servants went barefoot; the sandals showed he was a son, not a hired servant.

mc.stem: Which of these is NOT one of the father's qualities listed in this unit?
mc.why: The father was patient, loving, forgiving, and had his priorities right.

mc.stem: In the Chinese artist's second painting, the father's mismatched shoes showed:
options: He did not care about his appearance
He was in such a hurry to reach his son that he grabbed the nearest shoes
mc.why: God is always anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile.

mc.stem: When the elder brother says "this son of yours," he shows that:
options: He is confused about the family
He refuses to call the prodigal his brother
He wants the father to punish himself
mc.why: The father answers, "your brother was dead and is alive again."

mc.stem: In Luke 15, the elder brother represents:
options: The Pharisees who grumbled about Jesus eating with sinners
mc.why: The younger son was lost in the far country; the elder was lost at home.

mc.stem: Why does the parable end without telling us whether the elder brother went in?
options: The hearers must write the ending with their own lives
mc.why: The open ending is an invitation to every religious person.

mc.stem: Fred Craddock's dying father wrote "I was wrong" because:
options: The church he had criticized kept right on loving him
mc.why: His room was full of gifts from people at the church; their shoes did not match.

mc.stem: The grandmother and the coin collection illustrate:
options: The elder brother's spirit, which ends outside the feast
mc.why: She lost her granddaughter for twenty years over sixty dollars.

mc.stem: Mrs. Jones healed her whole town by:
options: Embracing and forgiving Bertram before he could finish apologizing
mc.why: Like the father in the parable, she was anxious to love, quick to forgive, eager to reconcile.

sa.prompt: Explain the setting of Luke 15 and how the three parables answer the Pharisees' complaint.
sa.model: Tax collectors and sinners drew near to hear Jesus, and the Pharisees and scribes complained that He received sinners and ate with them. Jesus answered with three stories in which something valuable is lost, someone searches, and there is joy when it is found. The parables defend His mission of seeking the lost and invite the grumblers to join heaven's celebration.

sa.prompt: Explain the parable of the lost sheep and what it teaches about evangelism, using the Indiana town.
sa.model: The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and goes after the one lost sheep until he finds it, then rejoices, just as heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents. The sheep was lost through its own foolishness. Jesus came to seek and save the lost. In the Indiana town, a stonemason went house to house with a deacon, others joined, and hundreds came to Christ. The shepherd goes after the lost rather than waiting for them.

sa.prompt: Explain the three truths this unit draws from the lost things: nobody plans to be lost, some are lost and do not know it, and there is joy when the lost are found.
sa.model: Nobody plans to be lost; the sheep wandered one mouthful at a time. Some are lost and do not know it, like the three famous explorers who got lost in the back streets of London within fifteen minutes. And there is always rejoicing when the lost are found: the shepherd and the woman call their friends to rejoice, and there is joy in heaven and before the angels over one sinner who repents.

sa.prompt: Explain the parable of the lost coin, including how it differs from the lost sheep and the lesson of the diamond.
sa.model: A woman with ten silver coins lost one, lit a lamp, swept the house, and searched until she found it, then rejoiced with her friends. The coins may have been part of her dowry, like a wedding ring. The sheep was lost through foolishness, but the coin through someone else's carelessness. The lost diamond found in a telephone box shows that precious things and people can be lost under our own roof, and Christians can lose their sense of purpose.

sa.prompt: Retell the younger son's journey from request to return, explaining the cultural details.
sa.model: The younger son asked for his inheritance while his father was alive, which was like saying he wished his father were dead. He went to a far country and wasted it all. In a famine he fed pigs, unclean to a Jew, and longed for their food. Then he came to himself, remembered his father's hired servants had plenty, and set out to confess his sin and ask to be made a hired servant.

sa.prompt: Describe the father's welcome and his four qualities.
sa.model: While the son was still far off, the father saw him, had compassion, ran, embraced, and kissed him, something a dignified older man did not do. He cut off the son's speech and gave him the best robe, a ring, and sandals, restoring honor, authority, and sonship, then held a feast. The father was patient, always watching the road; loving, running before asking questions; forgiving, restoring him fully; and had his priorities right, caring most that his son was alive and home.

sa.prompt: Explain the story of the Chinese artist and the mismatched shoes, and what it teaches about God and about us.
sa.model: A young Chinese Christian artist first painted the father standing at the gate with folded arms and a stern look, and the missionary said he missed the point. In the second painting the father was running, with one red shoe and one blue shoe, because he grabbed the nearest shoes in his hurry to reach his son. God is always anxious to love, quick to forgive, and eager to reconcile, and He wants us to live in that same spirit.

sa.prompt: Explain the elder brother's response and why he is the key to understanding Luke 15.
sa.model: The elder brother was angry and would not go in to the feast. He called the prodigal "this son of yours," not his brother, and described his years at home as slavery. The father went out to him too and said, "Your brother was dead and is alive again." He represents the Pharisees who grumbled; the younger son was lost in the far country, the elder was lost at home. The open ending leaves every religious person to decide whether to go in.

sa.prompt: Explain how to live in the spirit of the mismatched shoes in the church, the family, and personal relationships, with one example of each.
sa.model: In the church, Fred Craddock's father criticized the church for years, but when he was dying his room was full of its gifts, and he wrote, "I was wrong." In the family, a grandmother demanded back a sixty-dollar coin collection and lost her granddaughter for twenty years, the elder brother's spirit. In personal relationships, Mrs. Jones embraced and forgave Bertram after her husband's accidental death and healed the whole town.

sa.prompt: Outline two ways to preach Luke 15 and explain the closing illustration of adoption.
sa.model: One way preaches all three parables as lost things: the sheep lost through foolishness, the coin through carelessness, the son through willfulness, and the elder brother lost at home. Another preaches the prodigal alone, focusing on the father who is anxious to love, quick to forgive, and eager to reconcile, closing with the question, will you go in? In the closing story, an adopted daughter's mother said, "I always forget"; so the Father receives prodigals without holding the far country against them.
